note: 89 studies across 29 specialties, with a coded taxonomy separating design limitations from output limitations.
title: Current applications and challenges in large language models for patient care: a systematic review

reading.body:
Covering 89 studies across 29 medical specialties, this review separates design limitations from output limitations using a coded taxonomy, rather than treating all shortcomings as one category.

That separation matters because the fix for a design limitation, such as a model architecture unsuited to a task, is different from the fix for an output limitation, such as a model producing an inaccurate answer despite being suited to the task. Conflating the two makes it harder to know whether a specific failure needs a different model or better prompting and oversight around the model that is already in use.

The review does not report which specialties among the 29 covered showed the strongest or weakest results, only that the taxonomy was applied across all of them.

explain_beginner: The question, looking across everything published on using large language models like ChatGPT directly in patient facing care, what are people actually building, and does the evidence say these tools are ready to be trusted with real patients. Clinicians and hospitals cared because after ChatGPT's public release they rushed to try language models for all sorts of patient facing tasks, chatbots, translated patient instructions, drafted clinical notes, but the pace of adoption was outrunning any clear sense of whether the outputs were reliable enough to use unsupervised. Reviewing 89 studies across 29 medical specialties, almost all published in just 2022 and 2023, the authors found the overwhelming majority, 94 percent, were testing chatbot style question answering with patients, but also found that in the vast majority of these same studies, close to 88 percent, the AI's answers were flagged as either incomplete or containing outright inaccuracies. What it does not settle is which specific clinical use cases might already be safe with light supervision versus which need heavier safeguards, since the review pooled very different specialties and use cases together, and the authors' bottom line reads as a blanket caution rather than a use case by use case verdict.
explain_business: For any organization considering deploying a general purpose large language model chatbot directly with patients, this review is direct evidence that unsupervised use carries a real, well documented error rate, with incorrect or incomplete answers each showing up in the majority of studies reviewed, so a human review step is not an optional safeguard but the current baseline expectation for safe use. The 43.8 percent rate of studies reporting unsafe or misleading content is a compliance relevant number for anyone weighing liability exposure from a patient facing chatbot, and the 42.7 percent non-reproducibility rate means the same question can get a different answer on a different day, complicating any claim of consistent quality over time. Choosing GPT-3.5 over GPT-4, the more common but less capable choice across the studies reviewed here, may be a place organizations are trading cost for reliability, worth revisiting given these quality figures. This is directly relevant right now to healthcare organizations piloting or already running chatbots for patients, and the review's own recommendation is to keep a human in the loop and press vendors for training data transparency until stronger evidence and regulation catch up with practice.
explain_practitioner: Method, a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines and pre-registered on PROSPERO, screening 4,349 initial records across five databases down to 89 included studies from 2022 to 2023 covering 29 medical specialties, using a data driven thematic coding approach rather than a statistical meta-analysis, with study quality rated using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Medical chatbot use cases dominated at 94.4 percent of studies, 84 of 89, with patient information generation next at 20.2 percent, GPT-3.5 was the model used in 53.2 percent of studies and GPT-4 in 26.6 percent, and on quality, 87.6 percent of studies reported non-comprehensive outputs, 87.6 percent reported incorrect outputs, 43.8 percent reported unsafe or misleading content, and 42.7 percent reported non-reproducible results across repeated runs of the same question. Rather than benchmarking one model version against another directly, the review's contribution is aggregating how consistently these named failure types recur across a large, specialty diverse set of independent studies. The authors state their conclusion directly, current evidence shows these models are not yet reliable enough for autonomous medical use, citing undisclosed training data in 40.5 percent of studies as one underlying cause, and they call for mandatory human oversight and stronger regulatory frameworks.
